s1.p3: In this example, we are using an arrow function, which by definition cannot be a constructor as it lacks the **⟦f2⟧** property.
s1.p4: It is a factory because it returns an object.
s1.p5: And this object will know nothing about the function **⟦f3⟧**. It will be an instance of **⟦f4⟧**.
s1.p6: ![ico-20 warn] A function can be either a factory or a constructor.
s1.p8: A necessary but insufficient (![ico-20 warn]) condition for a function to be a factory is the presence of the operator **⟦f0⟧**.
s1.p9: In this example, the function **⟦f3⟧** returns an object. Great, let’s see what it returns if we call it with the keyword **⟦f1⟧**:
s1.p10: The function **⟦f3⟧** can no longer be a constructor, and using the keyword **⟦f1⟧** has no effect on its behaviour.
s1.p11: The function **⟦f3⟧** creates instances of the constructor **⟦f4⟧**.
s1.p12: In this example, the function **⟦f3⟧** returns an array.
s1.p13: However, an array is an object, so the function **⟦f3⟧** is destined to be a factory and can never become a constructor.
s1.p14: The function **⟦f5⟧** returns a number (possibly NaN or ⟦f6⟧). Can we say that it is a factory? – No, because it returns **not an object**.
s1.p15: When called with the keyword **⟦f1⟧**, it returns an instance of **⟦f5⟧**.
s1.p16: The same applies if the function returns a string, or ⟦f7⟧, or ⟦f8⟧. You can check this for yourself.
s1.p17: In other words, the function will be a factory only if it returns an instance of **⟦f4⟧**.
